nrt.facts: Opened in 1978 · Approximately 60 kilometers from the city center · Tokyo’s main international gateway
nrt.hist: In order to share the pressure of Haneda's international line, the port was opened in Narita City, Chiba Prefecture in 1978. Its construction process triggered a long-term local residents' movement and is an important page in Japan's aviation history. Since then, it has been gradually expanded to three terminals and has been responsible for most of Tokyo's international routes for a long time.
nrt.now: Fun: Watch the planes at the observation deck of Terminal 1. If you have enough waiting time (more than 4 hours), you can take a 10-minute drive to Naritasan Shinshoji Temple to visit the old streets. Eat: The restaurant streets in Terminals 1 and 2 offer sushi, ramen, and eel rice. The Kawafyo eel rice on the Shinshoji Temple is a century-old famous restaurant. Buy: Buy cosmetics and electrical appliances at Fa-So-La duty-free shop. Narita Airport’s exclusive souvenir and animation peripheral shops are also worth visiting.
meta: It is recommended to arrive 3 hours in advance for international flights
nrt.desc: Disney Resort located in Urayasu, Chiba. The Cinderella Castle at the entrance has pink walls and blue spires. It takes about 15 minutes to get to Maihama from Tokyo Station on the Keiyo Line.
details: Terminal Guide

T1 (mainly Star Alliance): 5F observatory, Pokémon store and animation area, the station is in B1; T2 (ANA, etc.): 4F commercial floor is densely packed with shops, and B1 has a capsule hotel for nine hours; T3 is an LCC dedicated terminal with simple facilities. It takes about 10 minutes to walk to T2. The observation deck at T1 is a good place to watch planes take off and land, and you can go shopping if you have a long layover.
Comparison of transportation into the city

The fastest Keisei Skyliner to Nippori and Ueno is 41 minutes, about ¥2,570 (all reserved seats); the Access Express to Asakusa and Shinagawa is about ¥1,270 and up; the Narita Express N'EX to Tokyo Station is about 53 minutes and about ¥3,070 (foreign tourists preferentially choose when round-trip discount tickets are more cost-effective); the highway bus to Tokyo Station is about ¥1,300 and up, 75–100 Minutes and most luggage friendly. Choosing a route based on accommodation location is more important than just time.
Practical tips

Transfer or long waiting time: a half-day trip to Naritasan Shinshoji Temple (get off at Keisei-Narita Station, the old street is famous for eel rice, and it takes 10 minutes by train from the airport); large luggage can be sent to the hotel via airport express delivery (next day delivery); please arrive 3 hours in advance for your return flight, as the morning is the peak time for T1/T2 security check.

toudai.facts: Founded in 1877 · Japan’s first national university · Hongo Campus: Akamon, Yasuda Lecture Hall, Ginkgo Avenue
toudai.hist: Its predecessor was the merger of Tokyo Kaisei School and Tokyo Medical School in 1877, making it the first modern university in Japan. Akamon was built in 1827 as the guardian gate of the Kaga Domain to marry the shogun's daughter. It is now a national important cultural property and a symbol of Todai. Yasuda Lecture Hall was donated by industrialist Zenjiro Yasuda and completed in 1925. Its Gothic clock tower dominates the skyline of the Hongo campus. Natsume Soseki's novel "Sanshiro" gave the school's heart character pond the name "Sanshiro Pond".
toudai.now: [Play] Enter the school from Akamon, walk along Ginkgo Avenue to Yasuda Lecture Hall, and then go around Sanshiro Pond and the General Library; the ginkgo is most beautiful in late November when it turns yellow. [Eat] The central cafeteria on campus is open to the public, and you can get student meals for a few hundred yen; there are also long-established soba noodles and cafes in Hongo-sanchome. [Buy] Dongda Students’ Association (cooperative) has Dongda-limited stationery, chocolates and ‘Akamon’ themed peripherals, which are difficult to buy outside the campus.
toudai.desc: Japan's first national university, the Hongo Campus' Akamon, Yasuda Lecture Hall and Ginkgo Avenue are the most bookish scenery in Tokyo. The campus can be visited freely.
details: Campus tour route

You can freely visit the entire campus (the interior of the teaching building is generally not open): Akamon (south side) → Ginkgo Avenue → Yasuda Lecture Hall → Comprehensive Library → Sanshiro Pond → Exit from the main gate or Longgang Gate, the whole journey takes about 1 hour. The interior of Yasuda Lecture Hall is only open during entrance ceremonies, graduation ceremonies and public events. You can usually look at the building and clock tower.
Architectural highlights

Yasuda Lecture Hall (1925): A Gothic Revival building designed by Shozo Uchida, the central clock tower is a symbol of the town, and Yasuda Zenjiro's donation was initially anonymous. Akamon (1827): The vermilion lacquered main entrance to the daimyo's residence in the Edo period, one of the only remaining shuden gates in Tokyo. The fountain square and Gothic arches in front of the comprehensive library are the most photogenic corners of the school; don’t miss the ginkgo trees in front of the lecture hall in autumn.
Practical tips

Transportation: Take the Marunouchi Line/Oedo Line 'Hongo-sanchome' station, or the North-Nan Line 'Higashidai-mae' station, just exit the station. Side trip: It takes about 15 minutes to walk to Ueno Park, and Nezu Shrine is also within the walking circle. You can arrange a half-day cultural tour of "Ueno Museum + Tokyo University Campus". Please keep quiet in the school and do not enter the teaching area to take pictures.

waseda.facts: Founded by Okuma Shigenobu in 1882 · Okuma Lecture Hall and 125-foot Bell Tower · One of Japan’s two private buildings
waseda.hist: It was founded as Tokyo Vocational College in 1882 by Okuma Shigenobu, the founder of the Meiji period. In 1902, it was renamed Waseda University. Together with Keio, it is known as one of Japan's top private schools. Okuma Lecture Hall is a Tudor Gothic auditorium built in 1927 to commemorate the 45th anniversary of its founding. The clock tower is 125 feet (approximately 38 meters) high - derived from Okuma's '125 years of life' longevity theory. The Tsubouchi Xiaoyao Memorial Acting Museum (1928) is a rare theater-specific museum in Asia, and the Murakami Haruki Library will open in 2021 with a collection of books donated by alumnus Haruki Murakami and designed by Kengo Kuma.
waseda.now: [Play] Okuma Lecture Hall and Bronze Statue → Okuma Garden (remains of the Edo Daimyo Garden) → Theater Museum (free) → Murakami Haruki Library (free, with coffee and reading space). [Eat] Just outside the school gate is the student street: a fierce battle area for ramen, fried noodles, affordable set meals, and student cafeterias on both sides of Okuma Avenue. [Buy] The on-campus student association has limited-edition merchandise for early-school students; the ‘Waseda Festival’ in early November is the largest school festival in Japan, and the whole street is lined with stalls.
waseda.desc: The prestigious private school founded by Okuma Shigenobu, the bell tower of Okuma Lecture Hall, the Drama Museum and Murakami Haruki Library are all on the Waseda campus, and outside the school gate is a lively student street.
details: Campus tour route

Free campus tour: Main entrance → Okuma Shigenobu Bronze Statue → Okuma Lecture Hall → Okuma Garden → Drama Museum → Murakami Haruki Library, about 1 hour. The interior of the Okuma Lecture Hall is only open on event days; admission to the Theater Museum and Haruki Murakami Library is free (the Haruki Murakami Library is occasionally closed, so check the official website before traveling).
Architectural highlights

Okuma Lecture Hall (1927): Tudor Gothic auditorium. The 125-foot bell tower corresponds to Okuma Shigenobu's "125 Years of Life Theory". The Kazami Rooster on the top of the tower is a symbol in the hearts of early students. The Theater Museum is modeled after the Fortune Theater in London in the 16th century. Its white walls and black wood appearance are unique among Japanese universities. Okuma Garden retains the pond and rockery of the daimyo's mansion garden in the Edo period, and is an oasis in a high-rise area.
Practical tips

Transportation: Walk for 5 minutes from ‘Waseda’ Station on the Tozai Line, or take the nostalgic Toden Arakawa Line to ‘Waseda’ Station (the old train itself is worth experiencing). On the way: Takadanobaba is about a 15-minute walk (ramen and Tezuka Osamu murals), and Kagurazaka Old Street is also within a walk and bus ride. The Waseda Festival (early November) is extremely popular and the area around campus is very crowded on those two days.

fuji.facts: 3,776 meters above sea level · Japan’s highest peak · Listed as a World Cultural Heritage in 2013 · Last erupted in 1707
fuji.hist: Mount Fuji is a stratovolcano formed by repeated eruptions. The current cone was formed about 10,000 years ago. The last eruption was the Hoei eruption in 1707. The ancients regarded climbing Mount Fuji as a spiritual practice. During the Edo period, followers of "Fujido" spread throughout Kanto, and the Sengen Shrine at the foot of the mountain was the center of belief. It is also an eternal motif of Japanese art - Katsushika Hokusai's "Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji" and Utagawa Hiroshige's Ukiyo-e paintings make it world-famous. In 2013, it was listed as a World Cultural Heritage as an ‘object of faith and a source of art’.
fuji.now: 【Play】Mountain viewing: Lake Kawaguchi (Oishi Park, Lakeside Fuji Fuji), Arakurayama Sengen Park Five-Storied Pagoda, Oshino Hakkai, one day is enough; Mountain climbing: the most classic way to go to Yoshidaguchi during the first mountain period (early July to early September), most people sleep one night in the 78th station mountain hut to watch the sunrise. [Eat] Yamanashi local noodle ‘Hofu (ほうとう)’ is pumpkin and vegetable miso noodles. The old shops in front of Kawaguchiko Station are the most famous; there are also desserts and puddings shaped like Mount Fuji. [Buy] Kawaguchiko Station and 5th station stores: Mount Fuji-limited cookies, yokan, sake, and hiking commemorative wooden staff imprints (a ritual exclusive for climbers).
meta: It is recommended to spend a whole day to see the mountain · 2 days for climbing
fuji.desc: Japan's highest peak (3,776 meters), located approximately 100 kilometers southwest of Tokyo, location indicated on the map. At the foot of the mountain are Lake Kawaguchi and Mount Arakura Five-Storied Pagoda - the most classic angles to see Mount Fuji are in this area.
details: How to get there from Tokyo

Viewing the mountains (in the direction of Lake Kawaguchi): Take the express bus from Shinjuku Station directly to Lake Kawaguchi Station for about 2 hours (about ¥2,200 reference, reservation required); the railway is from JR Chuo Line to Otsuki and transfer to the Fujikyu Line. The limited express "Fuji Express" can go directly from Shinjuku to Lake Kawaguchi (about 2 hours). Mountaineering: During the first mountaineering period, there are buses from Shinjuku/Lake Kawaguchi directly to the Yoshidaguchi 5th station (elevation 2,300 meters). Self-driving is the most flexible, but the parking lot at the fifth station is subject to restrictions during the climbing season.
Mountaineering Guide (Yoshidaguchi)

The mountain opening period is generally from early July to early September. In other seasons, mountain huts are closed and climbing is strictly prohibited. It takes about 5-7 hours to get to the top of the mountain from the fifth station of Yoshidaguchi and about 3-4 hours to go down the mountain. The current regulations for entering the mountain on the Yamanashi side: you need to make a reservation in advance on the official website and pay the entrance fee (approximately ¥4,000, subject to the official website of the year). There are gate controls from the afternoon to the early morning. "Forced climbing to the summit overnight" projectile mountaineering has been expressly prohibited and is very dangerous. Mountain huts must be reserved in advance. The temperature difference at the top of the mountain can reach 20°C, so cold protection and headlamps are a must.
Mountain Viewing Locations and Tips

Visibility rules: winter > other seasons, early morning > afternoon, the morning when it clears up after rain is best; you can check the "Mount Fuji Visibility Forecast" website before departure. Classic camera locations: Lake Kawaguchi Oishi Park (foreground during flower season), Arakurayama Sengen Park Five-story Pagoda (398 steps up, most crowded during cherry blossom and red leaf season), Lake Kawaguchi’s ‘Reverse Fuji’ reflection when there is no wind in the early morning, Lake Motosu (the location for the thousand-yen bill pattern). In Tokyo, you can see it from the Tokyo Skytree and Tokyo Metropolitan Government Observation Deck when the weather is good.

kamakura.facts: Next to Enoshima Electric Railway's "Kamakura Kogaku-mae Station" · In front of Kamakura Prefectural University Gate No. 1 · The location where the opening theme song of "Slam Dunk" was filmed · Facing Nanarihama and Enoshima
kamakura.hist: The Enoshima Electric Railway was opened to traffic in 1902 and was a small coastal railway running between Fujisawa and Kamakura; Kamakura Kogakumae Station was opened in 1931 (first name Hisaka Station). The intersection under the ramp in front of the station is opposite the gate of Kanagawa Prefectural Kamakura High School. In 1993, the scene of Sakuragi Hanamichi waiting for the train in front of the intersection and Haruko running from the opposite side in the opening theme of the animation "Slam Dunk" made this place famous overnight. The composition of the ramp, the green and white train and the sea has remained almost unchanged for more than 30 years. Now it is the first stop on the holy land tour in the hearts of animation fans around the world.
kamakura.now: [Play] Waiting at the crossing for the green and white Enoden train to pass by slowly (every 12 minutes) is a reenactment of the famous scene in the opening film; the seaside platform of the station itself is also a good place to see Enoshima; walk eastward along the coast to Shichirigahama and Inamurazaki, and you can even see Mount Fuji on a clear day. [Eat] Highly recommend Hase's earthen pot rice specialty restaurant "Kamakura Earthen Pot Kaedena.": Take Enoden 3 stops from the trailhead to Hase Station and walk for 3 minutes, right next to the Great Buddha Shrine. The Koshihikari rice produced in Tanba Sasayama is cooked pot by pot with kelp broth. The signature salmon roe clay pot rice and crab meat and avocado clay pot rice are all excellent. The set menu comes with 7 side dishes and miso soup. Lunch starts from about ¥2,800 and reservations are not available. There will be a long line when the door opens at 11 o'clock, while supplies last - please hurry up if you want to eat. The Shichirihama area is a sea-view restaurant area, and Bills is also famous for its waffles and the old-fashioned coral reef curry. [Buy] Kamakura Station Komachi Street is home to souvenirs such as Kamakura eagles and pigeon butter cakes, and Enoden peripheral products are on sale at Kamakura Station.
meta: It is recommended to clock in 0.5–1 hour · A full day tour of Kamakura/Enoshima
kamakura.desc: The railway crossing facing the sea at the beginning of "Slam Dunk" - in front of Kamakura Prefectural High School and next to the Enoshima Electric Railway Kamakura High School Front Station. Located approximately 55 kilometers southwest of Tokyo, the location is indicated on the map.
details: Check-in crossing: camera location and etiquette

The classic camera position is on the upper section of the ramp: stand on the inside of the sidewalk and use 2x zoom to bring the crossing, tram and sea into the same frame. The train runs about every 12 minutes, and when the alarm sounds, it retreats outside the railing and waits for the train to pass. Traffic wardens are on site year-round - do not stand in the middle of a driveway or on the tracks to take photos, and do not block ramps for residents to enter and exit. In the morning, there is good light and the water is the bluest; in the evening, the backlight is suitable for shooting silhouettes and sunsets. If you want to avoid the crowds, choose before 9 a.m. on weekdays.
Highly recommended food: Kaedena, a specialty earthen pot rice restaurant.

This is the most worth a special trip to eat at this restaurant. The owner is from Washoku Itamae and is located on the second floor of Hase Station, a 3-minute walk from Hase Station (3-8-13 Kamakura Nagaya). It is just 3 stops away from Kamakura Kogakumae by taking the Enoden Express, right next to the approach to the Great Buddha and Hase-dera Temple. The rice is Koshihikari rice delivered directly from contracted farmers in Tanba Sasayama, Hyogo Prefecture. It is put into the pot after receiving the order, and is cooked pot by pot with kelp stock over an open fire. The grains are distinct and full of umami flavor. The signature dish is the earthen pot rice with grilled salmon and pickled salmon roe. The crab meat, avocado, white fish (しらす) and seasonal items are also very popular. The set meal includes 7 side dishes and miso soup, and lunch starts from ¥2,800 (reference price). Note: Reservations are not available for lunch, and there are only 24 seats. There are people queuing up before the door opens at 11:00 (order first when queuing up). The restaurant is sold out while supplies last, so be sure to get there early if you want to eat. Dinner is a claypot rice set that is completely reservation-free (tel: 0467-25-3770). It is closed irregularly, mostly on Mondays. It’s firmly ranked among the more than 1,500 restaurants in Kamakura on TripAdvisor (4.6 points), and it’s a restaurant that even locals line up for.
How to get there from Tokyo · Tickets (prices are for reference only)

The smoothest way to go: Take the JR Yokosuka Line from Tokyo or Shinagawa to Kamakura (about 55–60 minutes), then change to the Enoshima Electric Railway to Kamakura Kozenmae for about 15 minutes. The one-way total is about ¥1,200 (IC reference price). Starting from Shinjuku, you can buy the Odakyu "Enoshima Kamakura Free Pass" (from Shinjuku for ¥1,640, including Odakyu round trip + unlimited rides on all Enoden lines). If you only travel along the Enoden Line, the 1-day pass "のりおりくん" is the most cost-effective for ¥800 (children ¥400). You can get on and off at Hase, Enoshima, and Inamurazaki as you like.
Side trip: Enoshima + Kamakura

Take two stops to the west to Enoshima Station, walk across the Benten Bridge to reach the island: Eshima Shrine, Iwaya Cave and Sea Candle Observation Lighthouse, half a day is just right. On the return trip, get off at Hase Station to see the Kamakura Big Buddha and Hase Temple, and finally return to Kamakura Station to visit Komachi Street to finish the day. On a clear morning in winter, you can see Mount Fuji floating on the sea from Shichirigahama to Inamurazaki. It is the most classic "sea and Fuji" in Kanto.

yokohama.facts: 296 m tall · Opened 1993 · Ferris wheel Ø 100 m · Red Brick Warehouse built 1911
yokohama.hist: This was once a Mitsubishi shipyard and a national-railway freight yard; from the 1980s it was reclaimed and rebuilt as the 'Minato Mirai 21' waterfront district. When Landmark Tower opened in 1993, its 296 m made it Japan's tallest building (until Abeno Harukas passed it in 2014). The stone dock at its foot is a Meiji-era dry dock, now home to the 1930 training sailing ship Nippon Maru. The great Ferris wheel was born at the 1989 Yokohama Expo and moved to its current site in 1999; the Red Brick Warehouses are Taisho-era customs sheds reborn in 2002 as shops and event space. One waterfront walk strings Yokohama's whole port history into a half-day stroll.
yokohama.now: 【Play】Start with Cosmo Clock 21 (¥1,000, about 15 minutes per rotation) for the harbour from 112.5 m up, then board the Nippon Maru (combo ticket with the Yokohama Port Museum ¥800), and finish on the grass deck of Osanbashi Pier at sunset. Landmark Tower's 69F Sky Garden is currently closed for the tower's renovation (reopening planned for 2028 or later), so for now admire the tower from the water's edge. 【Eat】Restaurants cluster in Landmark Plaza and Queen's Square; the Red Brick Warehouse has Yokohama Western-style classics and beer restaurants, and World Porters has a big food floor. 【Shop】Handmade goods at the Red Brick Warehouse and brands at Queen's Square; nearby, the Cup Noodles Museum lets you make your own cup noodles.
yokohama.desc: A harbour new town 30 km south of Tokyo: the 296 m Landmark Tower steps up beside the port, the 1930 sailing ship Nippon Maru rests at its foot, the 100 m Cosmo Clock 21 turns across the inlet, and the 1911 Red Brick Warehouses stand to the south. The whole bayfront lights up at night.
details: Landmark Tower & the Sky Garden (currently closed)

The tower is 296 m and 70 floors, opened in 1993; its elevators ran at 45 km/h, then the fastest in the world. The 69F Sky Garden, 273 m up, looks out to Tokyo Skytree and Mt. Fuji on clear days; admission was ¥1,000 for adults. Please note: for the tower's large-scale renovation, the Sky Garden ended operation on 31 Dec 2025 and is closed, with reopening planned for 2028 or later. Until then, visit the free Dockyard Garden and Nippon Maru at the tower's foot, and photograph the tower from the harbour side.
Cosmo Clock 21 Ferris wheel

Cosmo World charges no entry fee — you pay per ride. Its signature wheel is 100 m across and 112.5 m tall, with 60 gondolas taking about 15 minutes per rotation for ¥1,000 (the four see-through gondolas cost the same). The wheel is itself a giant clock — the world's largest when it debuted in 1989 — and at night the whole rim lights up with LED shows, the star of the Minato Mirai skyline. The park has around 30 attractions, including the 'Vanish' coaster that dives toward the water.
Red Brick Warehouse & the waterfront walk

Warehouse No. 2 was built in 1911 and No. 1 in 1913 as customs sheds for the Port of Yokohama. Today No. 2 holds shops and restaurants (mostly 11:00–20:00) and No. 1 is an exhibition and event hall; entry is free, and the plaza between them hosts markets and seasonal events. A good walking route: start at Sakuragicho Station, cross the Kishamichi promenade to the Nippon Maru and Landmark Tower, follow the inlet past Cosmo World to the Red Brick Warehouse, and end with sunset at Osanbashi Pier — flat and easy, about half a day.

yanaka.facts: About 170 m long · Some 60 small shops · Sunset steps · Famous cat street
yanaka.hist: Yanaka and its neighbours Nezu and Sendagi — 'Yanesen' for short — are among the few Tokyo districts to survive both the 1923 earthquake fires and the wartime air raids with their old townscape intact. Yanaka has been a temple town since the Edo period, and the shopping street grew after the war as the neighbourhood's everyday market: butchers, greengrocers, deli counters, senbei shops and sundries, shoulder to shoulder. The steps at the east end face due west into the sunset — hence 'Yuyake Dandan', the Sunset Steps. And Yanaka is Tokyo's cat street: pet cats, shop cats and cat-goods stores have quietly made the whole street their territory.
yanaka.now: 【Eat】Start with the menchi-katsu duel: Niku no Sato's Yanaka Menchi (¥250) against Niku no Suzuki's Ganso Genki Menchi-katsu (¥280), both fried to order and eaten at the storefront. For sweets, a cat-tail donut at Yanaka Shippoya (from ¥150), and in summer a shaved ice at Himitsudo. 【Play】Claim a spot on the Yuyake Dandan steps for sunset; in spring, walk 10 minutes to Nezu Shrine for the azaleas (April festival; azalea-garden donation ¥500–1,000), and Yanaka Cemetery's cherry avenue is nearby. 【Shop】Cat goods, hand-baked senbei and old-school deli foods — shitamachi flavours you can carry home.
yanaka.desc: An old Tokyo townscape that escaped the fires of war: some 60 small shops along a 170 m street, the 'Yuyake Dandan' sunset steps at its east end, and temples and cats across Yanesen to the west. Walk down the steps, then graze on menchi-katsu as you stroll.
details: Yuyake Dandan & the shopping street

Five minutes from JR Nippori Station's west exit, climb the steps and turn around: the street's sign arch and 170 m of shops run straight west, and at dusk the whole street turns gold — that is how the 'Sunset Steps' got their name. Cats often nap on the steps, so watch your feet. Down the steps and through the arch is the shopping street: around 60 shops, mostly serving locals at local prices. Come after 4 pm, watch the sunset first, then work your way along the shops and leave from Sendagi Station on the Chiyoda Line — a stroll with no backtracking.
The menchi-katsu duel & snack map

Yanaka Ginza's headline act is always the two butchers. Just below the steps, Niku no Sato sells the 'Yanaka Menchi' (¥250; domestic beef-and-pork mince, the juicy one); mid-street, Niku no Suzuki (founded 1933) sells the 'Ganso Genki Menchi-katsu' (¥280; bigger, bolder seasoning). The standard play is one of each, eaten hot at the storefront before you walk on — in Japanese shopping streets you don't eat while walking. For dessert, a cat-tail donut at Yanaka Shippoya (from ¥150), and in summer the famously queued shaved ice at Himitsudo — avoid the noon peak.
Wider Yanesen: Nezu Shrine & Yanaka Cemetery

Ten minutes south of the street is Nezu Shrine, said to have been founded about 1,900 years ago by Yamato Takeru and moved to its present site in 1705 by Tokugawa Tsunayoshi; the main hall is a Gongen-style Important Cultural Property, and Otome Inari Shrine inside has a tunnel of small vermillion torii. Its famous season is spring: the azalea garden's roughly 100 varieties and 3,000 bushes cover the slope in April, with a ¥500–1,000 garden donation during the Bunkyo Azalea Festival (varies with the bloom); the shrine grounds themselves are free. In the other direction, Yanaka Cemetery holds the grave of Tokugawa Yoshinobu, the last shogun, and a cherry-tree avenue loved by locals.

ghibli.facts: Reservation only · No tickets sold on site · 10:00–18:00 · Closed most Tuesdays
ghibli.hist: Opened in 2001 and designed by Hayao Miyazaki himself, the museum sits at the edge of Inokashira Park. Miyazaki wanted a museum "to get lost in": the building itself looks like a house from a Ghibli film — patchwork-colored walls, a spiral staircase, stained glass, and ivy-covered corners, with the 5-meter Robot Soldier from Castle in the Sky standing in the rooftop garden. Inside you will not find replicas but the real craft of animation: original drawings, manuscripts, and recreated workspaces. The Saturn Theater screens Ghibli short films shown only here.
ghibli.now: [See] First, the Totoro ticket window by the entrance (visible from outside). Inside, wander up the spiral stairs: exhibits on how animation works, a recreated Miyazaki workspace, the Cat Bus playroom (elementary-school kids only), and photos with the Robot Soldier on the roof. Your ticket stub admits you to one short film. [Eat] The Straw Hat Cafe is the only restaurant inside; hot dogs and fried chicken sets are popular and lines of 30 minutes are normal — go off-peak or eat after touring. [Buy] The Mamma Aiuto shop stocks many museum-exclusive goods: short-film merchandise, Robot Soldier figures, and Totoro plushies sell out often, so grab what you love.
ghibli.desc: Designed by Hayao Miyazaki, the museum hides in the greenery of Inokashira Park: patchwork walls, a spiral staircase, and the Laputa Robot Soldier in its rooftop garden. Strictly reservation-only; no tickets at the door.
details: Booking tickets (the important part)

Admission is by advance reservation only — no tickets are sold or booked at the museum. Tickets are sold solely through Lawson Ticket: sales open at 10:00 JST on the 10th of each month for the following month, with timed entry slots on the hour from 10:00 to 16:00 (arrive within one hour; you may stay until the 18:00 closing). Prices: ages 19+ ¥1,000; 13–18 ¥700; 7–12 ¥400; 4–6 ¥100; under 4 free. Weekend and holiday slots often sell out the same day; overseas visitors can use Lawson Ticket's English site or reputable travel platforms. The museum is closed most Tuesdays plus maintenance and winter breaks — always check the official calendar before booking.
How to tour the museum

Photography is not allowed inside (outdoors is fine) — putting the phone away actually helps you sink in. Suggested flow: first floor for the animation-craft exhibits and special exhibition → spiral staircase to the recreated workspace and the Cat Bus (adults may only watch; kids can climb in) → shop on the third floor → rooftop garden photos with the Robot Soldier → Straw Hat Cafe downstairs. Allow 2–3 unhurried hours. The theater's short film runs about 15 minutes and rotates through works, including Totoro side stories, that can be seen nowhere else.
Getting there and side trips

From JR Mitaka Station south exit it is a 15-minute walk, or take the community bus to Manjobashi. An even nicer approach: stroll about 20 minutes through Inokashira Park from Kichijoji Station — rent a boat on the pond first, then walk to the museum. Afterwards, wander Kichijoji's shopping streets and cafes, or head to the north side of Mitaka Station for sites linked to writer Osamu Dazai, who lived in Mitaka. Note: the Cat Bus room is for elementary-school children, and strollers are checked at the entrance.

kasukabe.facts: Hometown of Crayon Shin-chan · Nohara family statues at Kasukabe Station east exit · Ito-Yokado Kasukabe is the model for "Sato Kokonokado"
kasukabe.hist: Kasukabe, in Saitama, is the setting of Yoshito Usui's manga Crayon Shin-chan (serialized from 1990): the Nohara family lives here. Usui himself lived in Kasukabe for years, and the station Hiroshi commutes from — and the "Sato Kokonokado" department store where Misae shops — are modeled on Kasukabe Station and the Ito-Yokado store in front of it. Today bronze statues of the Nohara family stand at the station's east exit, and Shin-chan keeps popping up all over town. A perfectly ordinary suburb has become a pilgrimage site for Shin-chan fans worldwide.
kasukabe.now: [See] Start at the east-exit plaza with the Nohara family statues (all four, plus Shiro), then walk into Ito-Yokado Kasukabe and look for echoes of the anime's department store — there is a Shin-chan goods corner inside. Stroll the station-front shopping street for Shin-chan manhole covers and signs. With time to spare, take a taxi to the RyūQkan museum of the Metropolitan Area Outer Underground Discharge Channel and descend into the "underground temple" surge tank held up by 59 giant pillars (tour about ¥1,000, reservation required). [Eat] Local spots like Tobu Ramen near the station, plus a food floor in Ito-Yokado. [Buy] Kasukabe-limited Shin-chan goods and sweets at Ito-Yokado and station shops.
kasukabe.desc: The hometown of Crayon Shin-chan: bronze statues of the Nohara family at Kasukabe Station's east exit, and the Ito-Yokado store that modeled the anime's "Sato Kokonokado" — plus a visitable "underground temple" flood facility.
details: Pilgrimage route

From Asakusa in Tokyo, the Tobu Skytree Line reaches Kasukabe in about 40 minutes (also a Tobu Urban Park Line transfer station). Leave by the east exit: photos with the Nohara family statues in the plaza first, then a 2-minute walk to Ito-Yokado Kasukabe — the real store behind Misae's beloved "Sato Kokonokado"; a photo under the sign is the classic shot. Wander back through the shopping street hunting Shin-chan manhole covers. Everything is walkable in about 1.5–2 hours.
The underground temple: discharge channel

Kasukabe is also home to one of the world's largest underground flood-control facilities. The surge tank of the Metropolitan Area Outer Underground Discharge Channel is 177 m long and 78 m wide, roofed by 59 pillars 18 m tall — standing in it feels like a sci-fi temple. Fifty meters underground, it regulates five rivers to protect Tokyo from floods. The RyūQkan visitor facility is in the Showa district, about 15 minutes by bus or taxi from Kasukabe Station; tank tours must be booked on the official site (about ¥1,000) and can be cancelled in flood season.
Tips for Shin-chan fans

The statues are at the EAST exit — do not wander out the west side. Ito-Yokado is a real, working department store, so be mindful of local shoppers when taking photos. Shin-chan elements keep multiplying — station announcements, tour buses, sightseeing maps — and treasure-hunting them is half the fun. Kasukabe itself is a quiet residential town: do not expect a theme park. Its charm is that the Noharas' everyday life really happens here.

dome.facts: Opened 1988 · Japan's first all-weather dome · Home of the Yomiuri Giants · About 55,000 for concerts
dome.hist: Its predecessor was Korakuen Stadium. When it opened in March 1988, the white round roof earned it the nickname "BIG EGG": the roof is held up not by columns but by air pressure — the interior is kept about 0.3% above outside pressure, gently "inflating" the Teflon membrane, which is why the entrances use revolving doors to stop leaks. It was Japan's first all-weather multi-purpose stadium, hosting baseball plus concerts, martial arts, and exhibitions; in Japan people even measure areas in "Tokyo Domes," making it a national yardstick.
dome.now: [See] If there is a game, catch the Giants at home (or a concert); otherwise head to Tokyo Dome City Attractions: the centerless Big O Ferris wheel, the Thunder Dolphin coaster that dives through a building, then a soak at Spa LaQua. [Eat] Restaurants cluster in Dome City and LaQua; stadium food with a beer is the game-day classic. [Buy] Giants merchandise at the official shop, and baseball fans should not miss the Baseball Hall of Fame and Museum inside.
dome.desc: Japan's first all-weather domed stadium (1988), home of the Yomiuri Giants. Its white roof is held up by air pressure; next door, Tokyo Dome City packs in rides and a spa.
details: Games and events

During baseball season (late March–October) the Giants play at home almost every week. Reserved seats start around ¥2,300, varying by seat and opponent; popular games and concerts require early booking on official channels. On non-game days there are exhibitions and big events — check the official schedule first.
Tokyo Dome City Attractions

Entry is free and rides are pay-per-ride; a one-day pass for adults is about ¥4,500 on weekdays. Stars of the park: the Big O, the world's first centerless Ferris wheel (about ¥1,000, with karaoke gondolas), and Thunder Dolphin (about ¥1,800) — at 130 km/h it threads straight through the LaQua building before its plunge, the wildest coaster in central Tokyo.
Practical tips

Access: Suidobashi Station (JR Chuo-Sobu Line / Toei Mita Line) or Korakuen Station (Marunouchi / Namboku Lines), both steps away. Arrive an hour before a game for batting practice and merchandise. Spa LaQua stays open late into the night — perfect after a night game.

stadium.facts: Completed 2019 · Designed by Kengo Kuma · Main stadium of the Tokyo Olympics · About 68,000 seats
stadium.hist: It stands on the site of the 1964 Olympic stadium. Kengo Kuma's concept was a "Stadium in the Forest": the height is held to about 47 m, and the latticework of its five eaves tiers uses cedar and larch from all 47 prefectures — echoing how the Meiji Shrine forest was planted with donated trees from across Japan. Seen from the Gaien greenery it reads less like a giant arena and more like a gently rolling forest canopy. In the summer of 2021 it hosted the Tokyo Olympics' opening and closing ceremonies and the athletics events.
stadium.now: [See] The fifth-floor "Sora no Mori" sky corridor is free to enter: walk the ring for Shinjuku skyline views, and on clear days even Mt. Fuji. Scheduled stadium tours (book on the official site) take you through the athletes' tunnel and pitch side. [Eat] The surrounding Gaien, Aoyama, and Sendagaya neighborhoods offer cafes and longstanding soba shops. [Buy] The tour shop carries national-team and Olympic-legacy goods.
stadium.desc: The main venue of the Tokyo 2020 Olympics. Kengo Kuma's "Stadium in the Forest" wraps itself in five eaves tiers of timber from all 47 prefectures and melts into the Gaien greenery.
details: Architecture highlights

The five eaves tiers are the essence: timber from the 47 prefectures is arranged by compass direction, and the wooden lattice shades the sun while drawing in breezes. The roof is a wood-and-steel hybrid truss. The roughly 68,000 seats mix five greens, whites, and earth tones so from above they look like light dappling a forest floor. Using about 2,000 m³ of domestic timber, it is among the world's largest timber-using stadiums.
How to visit

The Sora no Mori corridor (outer ring, 5F) is free and open year-round, even without a game. For the inside, book a stadium tour on the official site: athletes' tunnel, locker rooms, and the edge of the pitch, mainly on non-match days. The ginkgo avenue of Meiji Jingu Gaien is right next door — in late November its gold pairs perfectly with the stadium on one walk.
Practical tips

Toei Oedo Line Kokuritsu-Kyogijo Station, exit A2, is right there; JR Sendagaya Station is a 5-minute walk. Chain it into a half-day stroll: Meiji Jingu Gaien → National Stadium → Shinjuku Gyoen. On J.League or national-team match days the crowds heading home are heavy — check the schedule ahead.

kichijoji.facts: Inokashira Park swan boats · Sunroad shopping street · Harmonica Yokocho · Gateway station to the Ghibli Museum
kichijoji.hist: Kichijoji perennially tops "most desirable neighborhoods to live in" rankings, where the JR Chuo and Inokashira lines meet. Inokashira Park to the south opened in 1917, one of Tokyo's oldest suburban parks; its pond, woods, and Benten shrine form a green oasis that has been a date spot for generations. The Sunroad arcade and the narrow lanes of Harmonica Yokocho preserve the air of the postwar black market and now buzz with tiny bars and zakka shops. The Ghibli Museum sits at the park's west end, an easy walk away — Kichijoji is the arrival station for most museum visitors.
kichijoji.now: [See] Start with a swan boat on Inokashira Pond (about ¥800 per 30 minutes), then stroll through the park to the Ghibli Museum (separate booking required). Back at the station, dive into Harmonica Yokocho: zakka and sweets by day, a lantern-lit alley of tiny bars by night. [Eat] The original round menchi-katsu at Satou the butcher (about ¥200) always has a queue; Iseya by the park is a Showa-era yakitori institution. [Buy] Sunroad, Marui, and Atre for goods and gifts; Nakamichi-dori is treasure territory for indie shops and vintage clothing.
kichijoji.desc: The neighborhood Tokyoites most want to live in: swan boats on Inokashira Pond, the Sunroad arcade, and Harmonica Yokocho's bar lanes — also the gateway station to the Ghibli Museum.
details: Inokashira Park and the swan boats

The park centers on Inokashira Pond, with the Benten shrine and the Inokashira Park Zoo on its banks. Boats rent from the pier on the pond's west side: swan paddle boats about ¥800 per 30 minutes, rowboats a little cheaper. Cherry-blossom season (late March–early April) is the prettiest, when petals cover the water — expect queues on weekends. The urban legend that couples who row here break up is a joke about the goddess Benten's jealousy; locals tell it with a smile. The Ghibli Museum is a 10-minute walk from the park's west exit, so the two chain naturally.
Harmonica Yokocho and station eats

North of the station, Harmonica Yokocho is a maze of lanes grown from the postwar black market: dozens of tiny shops along passages barely wide enough for two people — zakka, gyoza, and sweets by day; standing bars and yakitori after dark, when the red lanterns come on. The must-eat list: Satou's original round menchi-katsu (crisp outside, juicy beef inside, always a line), Kozasa's yokan (sells out by morning), and Iseya's yakitori with a beer. The lanes are narrow and smoky — do not drag big luggage in.
Combining it with the Ghibli Museum

Kichijoji Station is the smoothest gateway to the Ghibli Museum: a 20-minute walk through Inokashira Park from the south exit, or an Odakyu bus to the museum stop. A good build: the museum's 10:00 slot → back to Kichijoji for Harmonica Yokocho lunch → afternoon boats on the pond and Sunroad shopping. The museum closes most Tuesdays while Kichijoji's shops rarely rest, so swap the order depending on the day.

teamlab.facts: Immersive museum · Wade through water exhibits · 8:00–22:00 · Online booking only · Running until the end of 2027
teamlab.hist: teamLab Planets opened in Toyosu in 2018. Meant to be temporary, it kept extending on the strength of its crowds — now to the end of 2027 — and expanded 1.5 times over in January 2025, adding areas like the Athletics Forest and the Catching and Collecting Forest. It is the sister of Borderless in Azabudai: where Borderless is "wandering among artworks," Planets is "immersing your body in them" — you go barefoot, wade through knee-deep water, and watch projected koi swim around your legs. It has collected major international tourism awards and become a must-stop for overseas visitors to Tokyo.
teamlab.now: [See] Do not miss the four classics: the knee-deep koi pond, the Infinite Crystal World of mirrors and light strands, the Floating Flower Garden of real orchids overhead, and the sphere-light room you lie down in. The 2025 Athletics Forest, all jumping and climbing, is a hit with kids. [Eat] teamLab's own ramen and sweets shops stand outside; Toyosu Market and LaLaport are a short walk away. [Buy] The exit shop stocks Planets exclusives; crystal-themed accessories go first.
teamlab.desc: Immerse your whole body in art: wade barefoot through knee-deep water as koi swim past your legs and an infinite crystal universe sparkles overhead. The immersive museum foreign visitors love most.
details: Tickets and booking (well ahead)

Tickets are sold online only; there is no box office. Adult prices are dynamic: from ¥3,800, rising toward ¥5,000 for peak slots; ages 13–17 ¥2,800; 4–12 ¥1,500; under 4 free; a queue-skipping Premium Pass is ¥12,000. Sales usually open about two months ahead with timed slots every 30 minutes; weekends and cherry-blossom season sell out, so book one to two weeks early. Hours are 8:00–22:00 (last entry one hour before closing), with occasional closed days — check the official calendar when booking.
What to wear (this matters)

You tour barefoot, leaving shoes in free lockers at the entrance. The water areas reach an adult's knees: wear shorts or trousers that roll above the knee, and avoid long skirts or trousers that will soak. Several floors are mirrors, so skirt-wearers should plan an inner layer. Some areas have strong light and slopes, and a few restrict entry for pregnant visitors and those carrying infants. Phones are allowed (a waterproof pouch is wise); mind your camera around the water. Allow about 1.5–2 hours.
Getting there and side trips

Three minutes on foot from Shin-Toyosu Station on the Yurikamome Line, or about 10 minutes from Toyosu Station. Afterwards: seafood at Toyosu Market, a foot bath at Senkyaku Banrai, then the Yurikamome to Odaiba. Do not mix up the museums: Planets is in Toyosu (the one with water); Borderless is in Azabudai Hills, and tickets are not interchangeable.

kawagoe.facts: "Little Edo" kurazukuri streetscape · Toki no Kane bell tower · Kashiya Yokocho candy alley · About 30 minutes from Ikebukuro
kawagoe.hist: In the Edo period Kawagoe was the castle town of the Kawagoe Domain, shipping goods down the Shingashi River into Edo and prospering enough to earn the name "Little Edo." After the great fire of 1893 burned a third of the town, merchants rebuilt in fireproof kurazukuri style — thick earthen walls under heavy black-tile roofs — which is today's Ichibangai street. The Toki no Kane bell has told the time since the early Edo period; the current tower is the fourth, rebuilt in 1894. One street stacks three eras: kurazukuri (Meiji), the Taisho Roman-dori (Taisho-era Western buildings), and Kashiya Yokocho (Showa candy lanes) — the most complete Edo streetscape near Tokyo.
kawagoe.now: [See] Walk Ichibangai's kurazukuri street: view the Toki no Kane (time it for a bell strike), step inside preserved storehouses like the Osawa House, then duck into Kashiya Yokocho for candy. With time, add Kitain Temple (¥400, with its 500 Rakan statues) and Kawagoe Castle's Honmaru Goten (¥100). [Eat] Kawagoe signatures are eel (old houses like Ogawa Kiku) and sweet-potato desserts; the giant fu-gashi stick in Kashiya Yokocho is the photo prop. [Buy] Wagashi from old houses like Kameya along the kura street, Kawagoe Tozan textiles, glassware — and a bag of Showa candy in the yokocho.
kawagoe.desc: "Little Edo" Kawagoe: kurazukuri storehouses, the Toki no Kane bell tower, and Kashiya Yokocho layer Edo-to-Showa streetscapes into one walkable town, about 30 minutes from Ikebukuro.
details: Ichibangai and the Toki no Kane

Ichibangai is Kawagoe's face: some 30 kurazukuri buildings — black tiles, thick walls, second-floor kannon doors — all still working shops selling wagashi, miso, knives, and coffee. The Toki no Kane stands mid-street beside Yakushi Shrine, about 16 m tall, ringing four times a day (6:00, 12:00, 15:00, 18:00). The classic photos are the bell itself and the full streetscape from the street's entrance. The street runs about 400 m; give it a slow hour. Kimono rental shops along the way start around ¥3,000 including hair styling.
Kashiya Yokocho and Kitain

From Ichibangai's north end, slip into Kashiya Yokocho: a stone-paved lane of about 20 candy shops — handmade sweets, fu-gashi, sweet-potato chips — in air thick with sugar; a Showa kid's paradise. Fifteen minutes south is Kitain: the birth room of Tokugawa Iemitsu and Kasuga no Tsubone's dressing room, moved here from Edo Castle (admission ¥400), and 538 expressive Rakan statues, among Japan's three great Rakan sets. On the way back, Kawagoe Castle's Honmaru Goten (¥100, closed Mondays) is one of the few surviving palace halls of its kind.
Access and money-saving passes

From Ikebukuro, Tobu Tojo Line express trains reach Kawagoe Station in about 30 minutes for roughly ¥500; Seibu Shinjuku Line's Hon-Kawagoe Station is closer to the old town. The smart buy is Tobu's Kawagoe Discount Pass Premium from Ikebukuro (¥1,200): discounted round trip plus a day of unlimited city buses and shop perks. In town, the Koedo loop bus day pass is ¥600 (single ride ¥220); the old town is a 15-minute walk from the stations, so all-walking works too. Give Kawagoe a full day, or pair it with Kasukabe for a Saitama day trip (about an hour between the two stations).

inagi.facts: Yomiuriland · Kanto's largest jewellumination · PokePark KANTO · Mecha statues at Inagi-Naganuma Station
inagi.hist: Inagi is a quiet residential city in Tokyo's Tama area holding two trump cards. One is Yomiuriland, open since 1964: a classic Kanto amusement park with the Bandit coaster and a gondola gliding over cherry trees. From late October to the following April its Jewellumination wraps the whole park in jewel-colored LEDs — among the largest illumination events in the Kanto region. The other card is anime: mechanical designer Kunio Okawara, born in Inagi, left full-scale statues of the Gundam, a Zaku, and the Scopedog from Armored Trooper Votoms in front of JR Inagi-Naganuma Station. In 2026 the world's first permanent outdoor Pokémon facility, PokePark KANTO, also opened at Yomiuriland.
inagi.now: [See] Yomiuriland by day for the Bandit and the rides; in winter, from 16:00 the park turns into a sea of jewel light, best viewed from the Sky-Go-LAND Ferris wheel. Pokémon fans head straight to PokePark KANTO: a roughly 500 m forest trail plus a town area (tickets include park entry and must be bought ahead). Next door, the HANA・BIYORI botanical garden (¥800) has a Starbucks wrapped in flowers and live otters, and connects to the Hanakage-no-Yu hot spring (from ¥2,300). [Eat] Plenty of food inside and around; the garden and onsen restaurants suit a slower meal. [Buy] The Trainer's Market in PokePark and the park shops carry shelves of exclusives; Inagi's specialty is pears (Tamagawa pears), sold by the station in autumn.
inagi.desc: Inagi, home to classic Kanto amusement park Yomiuriland — famous for its jewel-toned Jewellumination — and to PokePark KANTO, opened in 2026. Full-scale Gundam and Scopedog statues stand at Inagi-Naganuma Station.
details: Yomiuriland and the Jewellumination

Prices: entry alone is ¥1,800 for adults. The one-day pass (entry + unlimited rides) is ¥5,900 for adults, ¥4,700 for ages 12–17, ¥4,100 for ages 6–11 and 65+, ¥2,500 for ages 3–5. The afternoon pass from 15:00 (¥3,100 for adults) is the best value if you come for the lights. The Jewellumination runs October 29, 2026 to April 4, 2027 (confirm on the official site), produced by lighting designer Motoko Ishii with a theme color that changes yearly; cherry season brings a special "night sakura" edition. The Pool WAI water park is summer-only, and the Sky Shuttle gondola and some attractions cost extra. The park closes on irregular days — check the official calendar first.
PokePark KANTO

Opened in February 2026, this is the world's first permanent outdoor Pokémon facility, about 2.6 hectares in two parts: Pokémon Forest, a roughly 500 m woodland trail where some 600 Pokémon live, and a town area with a Pokémon Center, a Gym, two attractions, character greetings, and the Trainer's Market. Tickets include Yomiuriland entry and must be bought online in advance: Trainer's Pass from ¥7,900, Ace Trainer's Pass from ¥14,000 (different perks). Popular dates vanish quickly — this is currently one of the hardest anime tickets in Japan, so watch the official release one to two months ahead.
The mecha statues and getting there

In the plaza in front of JR Inagi-Naganuma Station (Nambu Line) stand three full-scale monuments designed by Kunio Okawara: an RX-78 Gundam, a Zaku, and a roughly 3.6 m Scopedog from Armored Trooper Votoms. Okawara is Inagi-born, and the city treats him as its ambassador — look for his design touches around the station. The statues are free to view, two stops from Yomiuriland. Access: from Keio-Yomiuriland Station, the Sky Shuttle gondola (about ¥300 one way) lands you at the park entrance; or buses from Inagi-Naganuma. Shinjuku is about 40 minutes away. A good build: statues at Inagi-Naganuma by day → the park in the afternoon → illuminations at dusk.
